outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the conjecture for all n remains open; the only in-window result touching its own quantity f(n) is an unrefereed arXiv preprint (Ai and Lian, 12 August 2026) that lowers the linear upper bound to ⌈(18n−23)/7⌉ for every n ≥ 2 and proves the 2n−2 value for bi-arborescences; no AI system involvement was found.
problem_asks: Whether, for every n (n ≥ 2 in the sources), every tournament on 2n−2 vertices contains every oriented tree on n vertices as a subgraph (not necessarily induced). Parts: (1) every tree shape on n vertices; (2) every orientation of each such tree; (3) every tournament on exactly 2n−2 vertices as host; (4) all n, not only large n. The lower-bound half (2n−3 vertices do not suffice, via a regular tournament and an out- or in-star) is part of the statement's sharpness and is recorded in the sources as known; the question as worded asks only the containment at 2n−2.

events.what_happened: Havet and Thomassé, 'Median orders of tournaments', Journal of Graph Theory 35 (2000) 244–256 (venue from a search snippet; the PDF was unreadable through this tool). Shows every tournament of order 2n−2 contains every arborescence of order n > 1, i.e. Sumner's conjecture for arborescences. Also reported (secondary sources) a general bound f(n) ≤ ⌈(7n−5)/2⌉ via median orders. The Wikipedia article (opened) records the arborescence result with these authors and year.
events.delivers: Sumner's conjecture for arborescences (trees oriented entirely away from a root, or entirely towards it): every tournament on 2n−2 vertices contains every n-vertex arborescence. Secondary sources also credit a general linear bound ⌈(7n−5)/2⌉ for all oriented trees.
events.remains: All oriented trees on n vertices that are not arborescences; the exact 2n−2 threshold for general trees.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the result; Havet and Thomassé are established graph theorists
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the result in a refereed journal (per citation; I did not read the journal version)

events.direction: Supports the conjecture: establishes the conjectured 2n−2 threshold for arborescences.

events.what_happened: Reid and Wormald (1983), cited by the Wikipedia article: every near-regular tournament on 2n−2 vertices contains every n-vertex oriented tree (polytree); also caterpillars of diameter at most four. Wormald (1983) gave a general bound n log₂(2n/e) and corrected Burr's 1980 claim (Wikipedia; search snippet). The original paper was not located.
events.delivers: Sumner's 2n−2 threshold for near-regular host tournaments, for all n-vertex trees (as stated in the Wikipedia article); for caterpillars of diameter at most four, per the same citation (host order not stated in what I read).
events.remains: Host tournaments that are not near-regular; all trees outside the caterpillar class.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture within a restricted host class.

events.what_happened: Häggkvist and Thomason (1991), cited by the Wikipedia article as giving the first linear bound: every tournament on a linear number of vertices contains every n-vertex oriented tree; secondary sources give f(n) ≤ 12n and f(n) ≤ (4+o(1))n, and a 'few leaves' form n+g(k). Original not located; search summaries attribute the path result differently (see disputes).
events.delivers: A linear-in-n upper bound on the host order for all oriented trees (constant 12, or 4+o(1) per secondary sources); a tree-with-k-leaves form n+g(k).
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 threshold for all n; sharp linear constant.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; a linear bound, not the 2n−2 value.

events.what_happened: El Sahili (2004, per the Wikipedia citation; the original was not located, and one slide deck also dates it 2004): every tournament on 3n−3 vertices contains every oriented tree on n vertices, using median orders.
events.delivers: f(n) ≤ 3n−3 for all oriented trees on n ≥ 2 vertices (secondary sources; see disputes on whether this was the best general bound).
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 threshold; the sharper linear coefficients of Dross–Havet (2018) and Ai–Lian (2026).
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; a linear bound.

events.what_happened: Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus, 'An approximate version of Sumner's universal tournament conjecture', arXiv:1010.4429 (submitted 21 Oct 2010, single version); Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 101 (2011) 415–447, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2010.12.006. Theorem 1.4 (read on ar5iv): for α>0 there is n0 such that for n ≥ n0 every tournament on 2(1+α)n vertices contains every directed tree on n vertices; and for fixed Δ, tournaments on (1+α)n vertices contain every n-vertex directed tree of maximum degree at most Δ (n0 depending on Δ and α).
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv; journal version JCTB 101 (2011).
events.delivers: Asymptotic form only: for n large, every tournament on (2+o(1))n vertices contains every n-vertex oriented tree; for trees of bounded maximum degree, the sharp (1+o(1))n host bound.
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 value for every n; the factor 2+o(1) is not 2.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; the authors are expert graph theorists

events.direction: Supports the conjecture asymptotically; does not reach the exact threshold.

events.what_happened: Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus, 'A proof of Sumner's universal tournament conjecture for large tournaments', arXiv:1010.4430 (submitted 21 Oct 2010, single version); Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 102 (2011) 731–766, DOI 10.1112/plms/pdq035. Theorem 1.1 (read verbatim on ar5iv): 'There exists n0 such that the following holds. Let T be a directed tree on n ≥ n0 vertices, and G a tournament on 2n−2 vertices. Then G contains a copy of T.' The paper's sharpness remark: a regular tournament on 2n−3 vertices has n−2 in- and n−2 out-neighbours at every vertex, so it contains no star with n−1 leaves all pointing out (or in).
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv; journal version PLMS 102 (2011).
events.delivers: The full conjecture for all oriented trees on n ≥ n0 vertices, in every tournament on 2n−2 vertices (subgraph containment). The paper does not make n0 explicit in the portion I read. The sharpness of 2n−2 is also recorded (star versus regular tournament on 2n−3 vertices).
events.remains: Every n < n0: the paper gives no small-n result; the Wikipedia article and secondary sources treat the small-n cases as open.

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; refereed by the journal; authors are expert graph theorists

events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for all sufficiently large n; the threshold is sharp by the 2n−3 regular tournament example.

events.what_happened: Mycroft and Naia, 'Unavoidable trees in tournaments', arXiv:1609.03393 (submitted 12 Sep 2016, single version); Random Structures & Algorithms 53 (2018) 352–385, DOI 10.1002/rsa.20765, online 9 Feb 2018 (journal details from a search snippet). Abstract (read): an oriented tree on n vertices is unavoidable if every tournament on n vertices contains it (same-order containment, a different quantity from 2n−2); gives a sufficient condition; almost all labelled oriented trees are unavoidable, confirming a Bender–Wormald conjecture; every tournament on n+o(n) vertices contains every n-vertex oriented tree with polylogarithmic maximum degree, improving Kühn–Mycroft–Osthus.
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv; peer-reviewed version in RSA 2018.
events.delivers: (a) Same-order unavoidability for almost all labelled oriented trees (containment in tournaments on n vertices, not 2n−2 vertices). (b) Host order n+o(n) for oriented trees of polylogarithmic maximum degree (asymptotic, class-restricted).
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 threshold for every tree; trees of large maximum degree; all n.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; authors are expert combinatorialists

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; the (b) bound is an asymptotic bound for a restricted class and does not address 2n−2 for general trees.

events.what_happened: Dross and Havet, 'On the unavoidability of oriented trees', arXiv:1812.05167 (submitted 12 Dec 2018, single version); Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 151 (2021) 83–110 (from a DBLP listing, not opened). Abstract (read): every arborescence of order n with k leaves is (n+k−1)-unavoidable; every oriented tree of order n ≥ 2 with k leaves is (3/2 n + 3/2 k − 2)- and (9/2 n − 5/2 k − 9/2)-unavoidable, hence (21/8 n − 47/16)-unavoidable; and (n + 144k² − 280k + 124)-unavoidable. A digraph is n-unavoidable if it lies in every tournament of order n. Uses median orders.
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv; JCTB 2021 version.
events.delivers: A linear upper bound ⌈21n/8 − 47/16⌉ on the host order for every oriented tree on n ≥ 2 vertices, plus k-leaf bounds (n+k−1 for arborescences; n+144k²−280k+124 for trees with k leaves).
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 threshold for all trees; the gap between about 2.625n and 2n−2.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; authors are expert graph theorists
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2021), per DBLP listing

events.direction: Upper bound consistent with the conjecture; does not settle the 2n−2 value.

events.what_happened: Benford and Montgomery, 'Trees with few leaves in tournaments', arXiv:2103.06229 (v1 10 Mar 2021; v2 11 May 2022; v3 5 Jul 2022; no journal listed on the arXiv page). Abstract (read): (i) for some constant C > 0, every (n+Ck)-vertex tournament contains every n-vertex oriented tree with k leaves; (ii) for each k there is n0 such that for n ≥ n0 every (n+k−2)-vertex tournament contains every n-vertex oriented tree with at most k leaves, confirming a conjecture of Dross and Havet. The abstract does not mention Sumner's conjecture.
events.delivers: For trees with a fixed number k of leaves (k bounded, n ≥ n0(k) for (ii)): host order n+Ck, and n+k−2 for the stated range. Restricted to trees with few leaves.
events.remains: Trees whose number of leaves grows with n (including stars); all n; the exact 2n−2 threshold.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; a class-restricted asymptotic bound, not 2n−2 in general.

events.what_happened: Benford and Montgomery, 'Trees with many leaves in tournaments', arXiv:2207.06384 (v1 13 Jul 2022; v2 11 Oct 2024); Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 170 (2025) 260–334, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2024.10.001, available online 15 Oct 2024 (WRAP record, read). Abstract (read from arXiv and WRAP abstract pages): Sumner's conjecture is stated as the motivating problem; (i) for every α > 0 and n ≥ n0, every ((1+α)n+k)-vertex tournament contains every n-vertex oriented tree with k leaves (an asymptotic form of a Havet–Thomassé conjecture); (ii) for every α > 0 there are c > 0 and n0 such that for n ≥ n0 every (1+α)n-vertex tournament contains every n-vertex oriented tree T with maximum degree Δ(T) ≤ cn; (ii) improves Mycroft–Naia for polylogarithmic maximum degree.
events.revisions: arXiv v2 11 Oct 2024; the JCTB version is online 15 Oct 2024 and in print January 2025. Dating uses v1.
events.delivers: For n large: host order (1+α)n+k for oriented trees with k leaves (asymptotic in n with slack αn); host order (1+α)n for oriented trees with maximum degree at most cn. Both are asymptotic and class-restricted.
events.remains: The exact 2n−2 threshold for all n; small n; trees with many leaves and maximum degree above cn together.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; authors are established combinatorialists at Warwick
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (online 15 Oct 2024; print Jan 2025)

events.time_since_posted: about 4 years (about 2 years to the journal version)
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; asymptotic and class-restricted; does not establish 2n−2.

events.what_happened: Bessy, Gonçalves and Reinald, 'Oriented trees in O(k√k)-chromatic digraphs, a subquadratic bound for Burr's conjecture', arXiv:2402.19351 (submitted 29 Feb 2024, single version; abstract read). Burr's 1980 conjecture concerns digraphs with chromatic number 2k−2 containing every oriented tree on k vertices. Result: chromatic number 8√(2/15)·k√k + O(k) suffices; for arborescences √(4/3)·k√k + O(k). The paper does not mention tournaments or Sumner's conjecture.
events.delivers: A subquadratic bound for Burr's chromatic-number function. Since a tournament on N vertices has chromatic number N, Burr-type chromatic bounds imply Sumner-type bounds for tournaments, but only of order k^(3/2): weaker than the linear bounds already known for Sumner's quantity. Moves nothing on f(n) for tournaments.
events.remains: Burr's exact value 2k−2; and Sumner's exact 2n−2 (not addressed).
events.direction: Different quantity (chromatic number of digraphs; a stronger-hypothesis form of Sumner's question). Consistent with the conjecture; does not change the tournament threshold.

events.what_happened: Aboulker, Havet, Lochet, Lopes, Picasarri-Arrieta and Rambaud, 'Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments', arXiv:2410.23566 (submitted 31 Oct 2024, single version; abstract read); The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 33(3) (2026), article P3.22, DOI 10.37236/13540, published 7 Aug 2026 (journal page read). Results: oriented trees of order n with k added universal vertices embed in every tournament on 2·3^((k+1)(2k+1))·n vertices; k-blow-ups of oriented trees embed in every tournament on 2^(10+18k)·k·n vertices. Restates that oriented trees are linearly unavoidable (Häggkvist–Thomason) and that all acyclic digraphs are not (Fox, He, Wigderson).
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv; EJC version 2026.
events.delivers: Linear-unavoidability bounds for two digraph classes that are not oriented trees (trees with added universal vertices; blow-ups of trees). Nothing new for oriented trees themselves. Discounted as a neighbouring problem: the constants are exponential in k and the classes differ from the problem's.
events.remains: Everything about oriented trees: the exact 2n−2 threshold and the linear constant for trees.

checked_by.who: The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (refereed journal)

events.direction: Not about the tournament threshold for oriented trees; neighbouring problem.

events.what_happened: Fan, Lu and Chen, 'A near-linear upper bound for Burr's conjecture', arXiv:2609.18175 (submitted 16 Sep 2026, v1; abstract summary read). Abstract summary: f(k), the least chromatic number forcing every oriented tree on k vertices, is at most ⌊31 log(k!)⌋, so O(k log k), via an absorbing-set method. A search excerpt of the proof section instead states a(d) ≤ 31·log(d+2) for d ≥ 5 with small cases a(1)–a(4) = 46, 58, 70, 78 by computation. I could not see the definition of a(d) and cannot confirm the two are the same quantity.
events.delivers: Per the abstract summary, an O(k log k) chromatic-number bound for Burr's conjecture. Since tournaments have chromatic number equal to their order, this gives a Sumner-type bound of O(k log k) for tournaments, which is weaker than the known linear bounds: moves nothing on f(n).
events.direction: Different quantity (chromatic number of digraphs); does not change the tournament threshold.

events.what_happened: Ai and Lian, 'An improved finite bound for oriented trees in tournaments', arXiv:2608.11667 (submitted 12 Aug 2026, v1 only; full text read as arXiv HTML v1). Defines f(n) as the least N such that every tournament on N vertices contains every oriented tree on n vertices. Theorem 1: every oriented tree A on n ≥ 2 vertices satisfies unvd(A) ≤ ⌈(18n−23)/7⌉. Lemma 3: every bi-arborescence on n ≥ 2 vertices is (2n−2)-unavoidable, where a bi-arborescence is a rooted oriented tree that is the union of an in-arborescence and an out-arborescence meeting only at their common root. Corollary 13: every non-bi-arborescence on n vertices with k leaves has unvd ≤ 4n−2k−4. The method refines the three-phase median-order embedding in Dross and Havet's many-leaf proof and uses El Sahili's embedding. Authors: Nankai University; funding from NSFC grants 12522117 and 12401456.
events.delivers: For the conjecture's own quantity f(n): an upper bound f(n) ≤ ⌈(18n−23)/7⌉ for every n ≥ 2 (coefficient 18/7 ≈ 2.571, below Dross–Havet's 21/8 = 2.625 and El Sahili's 3). For bi-arborescences, the full conjectured value 2n−2 (Lemma 3), covering the out- and in-arborescences as special cases. For non-bi-arborescences, the bound 4n−2k−4 in terms of the number of leaves k.
events.remains: The conjectured exact value 2n−2 for every non-bi-arborescence tree on n vertices; the gap between about 2.571n and 2n−2 for general trees; all trees outside the bi-arborescence class.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 months (posted 12 Aug 2026; no refereeing found)
events.direction: Upper bound on the conjecture's own quantity, with the conjectured value 2n−2 proved for bi-arborescences. It is not a counterexample and does not contradict the conjecture; for general trees the threshold is only linearly bounded.

disputes.summary: Häggkvist and Thomason (1991) are credited by Wikipedia with the first linear bound. Some search summaries credit the path result to Thomason alone (1986) and give different constants. I did not read the originals, so the attributions are unresolved.

Wikipedia says Mycroft and Naia (2018) confirmed the Havet–Thomassé strengthening (n+k−1 vertices for trees with k leaves) for almost every tree. The arXiv abstract I read describes almost all labelled oriented trees being unavoidable, meaning containment in tournaments of the same order n, and does not mention the Havet–Thomassé strengthening. These may concern different quantities; not resolved.

Some sources call El Sahili's 3n−3 the best known general bound. The Dross–Havet 21/8 (2018) and the Ai–Lian 18/7 (2026) bounds are smaller in the linear coefficient, so El Sahili's bound is superseded for general n. Recorded so the judging pass uses the events rather than these summaries.

summary: Sumner's conjecture (every oriented tree on n vertices sits in every tournament on 2n−2 vertices) remains open for general n. Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus (arXiv 1010.4430, 2010; Proc. LMS 2011) proved it for all n ≥ n0 with n0 not made explicit; I verified Theorem 1.1 verbatim on ar5iv, and it is the event on which the large-n status rests. Their companion (arXiv 1010.4429; JCTB 2011) gives only the asymptotic (2+o(1))n bound. Between these and the present, the linear bounds came from Häggkvist–Thomason (1991, secondary sources), Havet–Thomassé (2000, arborescences exact; general ⌈(7n−5)/2⌉ per secondary sources), El Sahili (2004, 3n−3, original not located), Dross–Havet (arXiv 2018, JCTB 2021, ⌈21n/8−47/16⌉), and the class-restricted asymptotic results of Mycroft–Naia (2016) and Benford–Montgomery (2021; 2022/JCTB 2025). None of these reaches 2n−2 for general trees. The only in-window result touching the conjecture's own quantity is Ai and Lian (arXiv 2608.11667, 12 Aug 2026, single version, no refereeing or public engagement found). I read its full HTML text: Theorem 1 gives f(n) ≤ ⌈(18n−23)/7⌉ for all n ≥ 2, and Lemma 3 proves the conjectured 2n−2 for bi-arborescences, a class containing all out- and in-arborescences. That is a partial result that moves a bound and settles a restricted class; for general trees the conjecture is unchanged. Close calls: (a) by the abc precedent, a bound on f(n) moves the conjecture's own quantity, so the Ai–Lian bound counts as movement, though not a resolution; (b) the two Burr-conjecture papers (Bessy–Gonçalves–Reinald, arXiv 2402.19351, 29 Feb 2024; Fan–Lu–Chen, arXiv 2609.18175, 16 Sep 2026) concern chromatic number of digraphs, which is a stronger-hypothesis form that implies a Sumner-type statement, but their bounds (k^{3/2}, k log k) are weaker than the known linear bounds, so they move nothing on f(n); (c) Aboulker et al. (arXiv 2410.23566, 31 Oct 2024; EJC 2026) concern other digraph classes and are discounted. AI search: I searched the problem name with AI terms (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, Erdős-problem and language-model acknowledgement searches) and the OpenAI release of 6 October 2026 (github.com/openai/math; 719 or 722 manuscripts in 372 families, produced by an 'unreleased internal OpenAI model', per the README). I scanned the CONTENTS.md manuscript map in chunks and found no tournament, oriented-tree, Sumner or Havet entry in what I could read. The scan tool truncated long chunks, so this is partial, not a full text search. The Ai–Lian full text has no AI or computational statement. The Benford–Montgomery PDFs and the Havet–Thomassé PDF returned binary and were unreadable, so their acknowledgements and AI statements are unchecked; the 'none found' answers for them rest on abstracts. Pre-2024 papers name no AI system. Other 2026 tournament papers with AI disclosures (arXiv 2609.13924, Claude; arXiv 2605.14138, ChatGPT Pro) concern other properties, not Sumner's conjecture.
competing_reading: Against counting Ai–Lian as a bound on the conjecture's own quantity: its 18/7 ≈ 2.571n bound stays above the conjectured 2n−2 for every n, its exact-value content is confined to bi-arborescences, and nothing in the window resolves the problem. For counting it: the abc precedent treats a bound on the quantity the conjecture names as moving it, and f(n) is that quantity. A second reading: Kühn–Mycroft–Osthus (2010) already settled the large-n case, so the in-window events add only a bound and a restricted class to a problem whose large-n status predates the window. A third: the 'bi-arborescence' class is narrower than it sounds, since it is the union of an in-arborescence and an out-arborescence meeting only at a root, and Havet–Thomassé had already covered the one-sided case.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or an independent re-derivation of Theorem 1 and Lemma 3 of Ai–Lian. (2) Full texts of Benford–Montgomery (arXiv 2207.06384; WRAP PDF) and the Havet–Thomassé PDF, to check the acknowledgements and any AI or computational statement, and to confirm what they claim. (3) An explicit n0 in Kühn–Mycroft–Osthus, or a later paper stating small-n verification, to settle the small-n status. (4) A complete read of openai/math CONTENTS.md, or a repository search for 'tournament', 'Sumner' and 'oriented tree', to close the AI search. (5) The Fan–Lu–Chen definition of a(d), to confirm whether its bound is the same quantity as the abstract summary's f(k).
